name: Antitrust Procedure Regulation
evidence_rating: thin: Commission evaluations based on enforcement records, consultation and a support study; no independent study of the Regulation's effect on enforcement outcomes
summary: Regulation 1/2003 ended the notification of agreements to the Commission and shared enforcement with national authorities and courts. The Commission's 2024 evaluation judged the framework broadly effective, citing 225 Commission enforcement decisions and more than EUR 42 billion in fines over 20 years, but found procedures slow and less suited to digital markets; a revision is under way.

indicators.objective: No monitoring indicators set in the proposal; assessed through the Commission's reports listed below
Effective and uniform enforcement of Articles 101 and 102
indicators.evidence: 2004-2024: 225 Commission enforcement decisions; fines above EUR 42 billion (about EUR 37 billion upheld by the EU Courts).

literature.citation: European Commission (2009), Report on the functioning of Regulation 1/2003, COM(2009) 206
literature.title: Report on the functioning of Regulation 1/2003
literature.outcomes: enforcement; cooperation in the competition network
literature.headline: Five years on, the Regulation had transformed enforcement: more cases by national authorities, cooperation through the European Competition Network, and an end to notifications
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's first review found the 2004 reform had made antitrust enforcement across the EU more active and better coordinated.

literature.citation: European Commission (DG COMP) (2024), Commission Staff Working Document: Executive summary of the evaluation of Regulations 1/2003 and 773/2004 (SWD(2024) 217 final), European Commission, Staff Working Document
literature.title: Commission Staff Working Document: Executive summary of the evaluation of Regulations 1/2003 and 773/2004 (SWD(2024) 217 final)
literature.method: Better Regulation evaluation: public consultation, internal ECN survey of NCAs, support study with 250+ expert interviews, desk research and Commission/NCA enforcement data
literature.outcomes: effectiveness and efficiency of enforcement; abolition of notification; ECN co-enforcement; investigative tools
literature.headline: Finds the Regulations effective overall: abolishing notification was 'remarkably smooth' and co-enforcement with NCAs through the ECN 'a success'. But digitalisation is weakening inspections and requests for information, interim measures and structural remedies are underused, and investigations are too long. Press summaries add 225 Commission enforcement decisions and over EUR 42bn in fines since May 2004.
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's own 20-year review says the 2004 reform that let national authorities enforce EU antitrust law has worked well, but its investigation tools are slow and ageing.
literature.quality: descriptive/qualitative self-evaluation; no counterfactual; Commission evaluating its own framework
literature.verified: full text read (executive summary SWD(2024) 217); decision/fine counts from secondary press and law-firm summaries only
literature.interested_party: European Commission (evaluating its own enforcement framework)

literature.citation: Wils, W.P.J. (2013), Ten Years of Regulation 1/2003 - A Retrospective, Journal of European Competition Law & Practice 4(4):293-301
literature.title: Ten Years of Regulation 1/2003 - A Retrospective
literature.venue: Journal of European Competition Law & Practice 4(4):293-301
literature.method: descriptive retrospective of enforcement activity and expectations from the 1999 White Paper
literature.outcomes: NCA activity; ECN functioning; Commission prohibition decisions; private enforcement
literature.headline: Calls the NCA/ECN enforcement system 'a major success, beyond expectations'. But the White Paper's forecast of a substantial rise in Commission prohibition decisions after notifications were abolished 'may have been too optimistic'.
literature.summary_plain: An insider's ten-year review finds that national competition authorities took up EU antitrust enforcement strongly, while the Commission brought fewer new cases than promised.
literature.quality: descriptive; expert assessment, no causal design
literature.interested_party: author affiliated with the European Commission (DG COMP) at time of writing

literature.citation: Bernatt, M.; Botta, M.; Svetlicinii, A. (2015), The assessment of the effect on trade by the national competition authorities of the 'new' Member States: Another legal partition of the Internal Market?, Common Market Law Review 52(5):1247-1275
literature.authors: Bernatt, M.; Botta, M.; Svetlicinii, A.
literature.title: The assessment of the effect on trade by the national competition authorities of the 'new' Member States: Another legal partition of the Internal Market?
literature.method: comparative legal-empirical analysis of NCA decisions and ECN notifications in selected new Member States
literature.outcomes: number of envisaged decisions notified under Art 11(4); use of EU vs national law; effect-on-trade assessment
literature.headline: New-Member-State NCAs notified fewer envisaged Art 101/102 decisions than old-Member-State NCAs. They were not less active, though: most of their decisions were adopted under national law, and their assessment of 'effect on trade' diverged significantly, sometimes ignoring ECJ case law and the 2004 Notice.
literature.summary_plain: Competition authorities in newer EU countries enforce actively but often avoid applying EU law, which undercuts the uniform enforcement Regulation 1/2003 aimed for.
literature.quality: descriptive; case-law and decision coding; small set of jurisdictions

literature.citation: Hellwig, M.; Hüschelrath, K. (2017), Cartel Cases and the Cartel Enforcement Process in the European Union 2001-2015: A Quantitative Assessment, The Antitrust Bulletin 62(2):400-438
literature.title: Cartel Cases and the Cartel Enforcement Process in the European Union 2001-2015: A Quantitative Assessment
literature.method: descriptive statistics on all EC cartel decisions 2001-2015 (duration, detection route, leniency, settlement, fines, appeals)
literature.outcomes: cartel characteristics; investigation duration; detection type; fines; appeal outcomes
literature.headline: Gives a comprehensive quantitative profile of every Commission cartel case decided in 2001-2015, including detection route, leniency, settlements, fines and appeals. The abstract does not attribute changes to Regulation 1/2003.
literature.summary_plain: A detailed statistical description of EU cartel cases spanning the 2004 reform, useful as background but not a test of whether the reform worked.
literature.quality: descriptive; does not isolate the effect of Regulation 1/2003

literature.citation: Ordóñez-de-Haro, J.M.; Borrell, J.-R.; Jiménez, J.L. (2018), The European Commission's Fight against Cartels (1962-2014): A Retrospective and Forensic Analysis, JCMS: Journal of Common Market Studies 56(5):1087-1107
literature.authors: Ordóñez-de-Haro, J.M.; Borrell, J.-R.; Jiménez, J.L.
literature.title: The European Commission's Fight against Cartels (1962-2014): A Retrospective and Forensic Analysis
literature.venue: JCMS: Journal of Common Market Studies 56(5):1087-1107
literature.method: forensic analysis of all published Commission cartel decisions 1962-2014, by policy stage
literature.outcomes: cartel detection and sanctioning across reform stages
literature.headline: Identifies the leniency programme, not the procedural modernisation, as the 'critical juncture' that let authorities detect and sanction cartels much more effectively.
literature.summary_plain: A long-run history of EU cartel cases credits leniency (immunity for whistle-blowing firms) more than the 2004 procedural reform for better cartel detection.
literature.quality: descriptive/historical; no causal estimate for Regulation 1/2003
